paragraphs.heading: Breaking things into factors
paragraphs.text: Factoring means rewriting a number, or some other mathematical object, as a product of pieces called factors. The pieces are usually smaller or simpler things of the same kind. The number 15 can be written as 3 × 5, for instance. In the same way, the polynomial x² − 4 can be written as (x − 2)(x + 2).

paragraphs.heading: Where it makes sense
paragraphs.text: In number systems where you can always divide, such as the real or complex numbers, factoring is not usually treated as meaningful. Any x there can be written as (xy) × (1/y) for any y that is not zero, so splits come cheap and say nothing. A fraction, or a ratio of polynomials, can still be factored in a useful way. You reduce it to lowest terms and then factor the top and the bottom on their own.

paragraphs.heading: Primes and the Greeks
paragraphs.text: Ancient Greek mathematicians were the first to study factoring, working with whole numbers. They proved the fundamental theorem of arithmetic. It says every positive integer splits into a product of prime numbers, which are numbers that cannot be broken further into integers greater than 1. That split is unique, apart from the order in which the factors are listed.

paragraphs.heading: Finding the factors of a number
paragraphs.text: To factor a whole number n, you need a way to find a divisor q of n, or to decide that n is prime. Once a divisor turns up, you repeat the search on q and on n / q until nothing more splits. It is enough to try values of q with 1 < q and q² ≤ n. If you try them in increasing order, the first divisor you find is always prime. For one even number n, taking out 2 gives n = 2 · 693, and taking out 3 twice gives n = 2 · 3² · 77.

paragraphs.heading: Easy to multiply, hard to undo
paragraphs.text: Factoring a whole number is a sort of reverse of multiplying, yet it is much harder for an algorithm to do. Simple trial division works for small numbers but bogs down for big ones. Pierre de Fermat never discovered that 4 294 967 297 is not prime, and checking it by this method would take more than 10000 divisions. Even the best current methods, on powerful computers, cannot factor a 500-digit number made by multiplying two randomly chosen primes. That difficulty keeps the RSA cryptosystem secure, and RSA is widely used to protect internet communication.

paragraphs.heading: Factoring polynomials
paragraphs.text: Polynomials have also been factored for centuries. In basic algebra, factoring a polynomial turns the job of finding its roots into finding the roots of each factor. Polynomials with integer coefficients factor in only one way into irreducible polynomials, which play the part that primes play for numbers. A polynomial in one variable with complex coefficients splits uniquely, up to order, into linear pieces, a version of the fundamental theorem of algebra.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond numbers
paragraphs.text: The word also covers splitting other objects into a product of simpler ones. Matrices, for example, have many kinds of factorization. One of them writes any matrix as a product of three matrices: L, which is lower triangular, U, which is upper triangular, and a permutation matrix P. This LUP form is Gaussian elimination written in the language of matrices.
